title: Async KV paging + op-fusion experiments
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a set of exploratory experiments and design notes for combining asynchronous paged-KV fetching with light-weight kernel/operator fusion in the serving runtime. The primary focus is minimizing p99 tail latency for long-context chat workloads while preserving high token throughput on A100/RTX-class GPUs. This is not a fully baked RFC — more of a lab notebook covering micro-scheduler ideas, admission-control heuristics, and short-term fusion prototypes.

Background / motivation:
- Paged KV reduces peak GPU memory by paging infrequently-used KV pages to host memory (or NVMe). But page faults / on-demand fetches can create high tail latencies if not carefully scheduled.
- FlashAttention (and its derivatives) are extremely memory-bandwidth sensitive; introducing uncontrolled asynchronous memcpy or host->device transfer during attention execution can thrash kernels.
- Prior work in this folder explored prefetching and eviction heuristics (see linked artifacts). This doc attempts to tie an async page pipeline to a micro-scheduler, and simultaneously fuse small ops to reduce kernel launch overhead during page fetch windows.

Goals / hypotheses:
1) Introduce a first-class async page fetch pipeline that exposes predictable latency and cancellable prefetches to the runtime scheduler.
2) Reduce p99 by ordering prefetches and attention kernels such that device compute is not starved by in-flight DMA for hot pages.
3) Gain a small but measurable reduction in per-token CPU overhead and kernel launch overhead by fusing bookkeeping kernels (KV indexing, small format conversions) into adjacent attention/fusion kernels during periods of no DMA.
4) Keep the change incremental: no model-rewrite required, compatibility mode that falls back to existing paged-KV behavior.

Design sketch:
1) Pipeline stages (logical):
   - Admission: request comes in with key/page refs (page ids for KV). The admission stage computes a predicted set of pages to touch given current prompt length and token distribution.
   - Prefetch controller: decides which pages to fetch now vs defer. Maintains a per-GPU prioritized queue; priority = weighted score(past-access-frequency, distance-to-past-prefix, model-layer-sensitivity).
   - Async fetch workers: dedicated host threads per-GPU that perform pinned-host reads and cudaMemcpyAsync into preallocated page slabs on device. Each transfer is associated with a CUDA event and stream.
   - Micro-scheduler: coordinates when to launch attention kernels on the main stream vs schedule small fusable ops on low-priority streams during idle windows.
   - Eviction: weighted eviction that avoids evicting pages likely to be reused within a short horizon.

2) Admission & scoring (notes):
   - Use a sliding-window frequency (decay factor 0.9 per token) to capture temporal locality.
   - Multiply by layer-sensitivity factor: early layers often touch KV pages more predictably; later layers have sparser reuse. These factors are empirically tuned per-model.
   - Score formula (toy): score = freq_score * decay_factor * (1 + alpha*layer_sensitivity) - beta*device_memory_pressure.

3) Prefetch batching and coalescing:
   - Coalesce multiple page reads into a single host I/O when pages are contiguous on disk/NVMe. This is important for NVMe-backed stores.
   - Use a target batch size (pages per batch) that trades off latency vs bus saturation. Empirically 4-8 pages per batch works well on our infra for 16k-context models.

4) CUDA stream/topology conventions:
   - Main compute stream (S_main): used for attention and heavy kernels. High priority.
   - DMA stream(s) (S_dma_low, S_dma_high): used for H2D memcpys. Use low priority for background prefetch. High-priority DMA reserved for on-demand page fault fetches that block a critical request.
   - Helper streams (S_helper): used for small fused prep kernels when no DMA is active. These run on low priority but can preempt background prefetch if needed.

5) Op fusion opportunities (conservative):
   - KV index remap + small dtype-conversion (fp16<->q8xx) fused into a single lightweight kernel that writes directly into the page slab on device, reducing an extra kernel and an extra copy.
   - Small bookkeeping kernels (slice/cat/reshape) fused into the attention prelude when the micro-scheduler detects no in-flight DMA on the device.
   - DO NOT fuse the full attention with DMA — that kills overlap. Only fuse when the prefetch controller reports page residency stable for the next N tokens.

Micro-scheduler behavior (prototype):
- Each incoming request attaches a page-hint vector (list of page ids and urgency). The micro-scheduler evaluates: are required pages resident?
  - If yes: schedule attention on S_main ASAP.
  - If no: check if pages are already in-flight: wait on their events. If in-flight and predicted completion <= latency-SLO, allowed to proceed; else, try to reorder non-dependent requests.
- While waiting for DMA, attempt to run fusable small ops (bookkeeping) on S_helper to avoid idle CPU->GPU syncs.
- If overall GPU utilization is low, allow speculative prefetch of low-priority pages on S_dma_low.

Eviction & memory pressure heuristics:
- Weighted LRU with a tiny fixed-size hotset (e.g., 2% capacity) pinned for 10s to avoid thrash during multi-turn chats.
- Evict pages with lowest predicted reuse score; tie-breaker = farthest layer distance.
- If device memory pressure crosses a threshold, transition to aggressive coalesced eviction (group evict contiguous pages to reduce fragmentation).

Experiments run (summary):
- Benchmarks: 8K and 16K context T5-style and Llama-2-13B mapping. 1 GPU (A100-40GB), NVMe backend for cold pages.
- Baselines: legacy paged-KV (synchronous blocking fetch), existing prefetcher (single-thread), and new async pipeline + fusion prototype.
- Key microbenchmarks (representative):
   * Legacy: 1k tokens/sec, p99 420ms
   * Single-thread prefetcher: 1.25k tokens/sec, p99 310ms
   * Async pipeline (no fusion): 1.3k tokens/sec, p99 240ms
   * Async pipeline + conservative fusion: 1.35k tokens/sec, p99 175ms
Notes: numbers are noisy; run-to-run variance +/- 6-12%. Fusion produced diminishing returns on pure-memory-bound attention, but helped when many small bookkeeping kernels were present.

Observations / learnings:
- The biggest wins come from better prefetch prioritization and reducing stalls waiting for critical pages; small fusions are nice but secondary.
- High-priority DMA for on-demand faults is necessary to keep p99 bounded for interactive workloads — background prefetch cannot be relied on for edge cases.
- Coalescing NVMe reads reduced I/O stalls by ~30% when many scattered pages were needed for context window sliding.
- Careful stream priority tuning is critical: if DMA uses the same priority as compute, we see throughput collapse due to memory bus contention.

Open questions / risks:
- How to set layer_sensitivity automatically per model without manual tuning? Can we learn it from a short warm-up profiling run?
- Fusion correctness surface: when dtype conversions and quantized layouts are involved we need bit-exactness checks across fallbacks.
- Multi-GPU scenarios: page placement and cross-GPU traffic add complexity; the scheduler must be topology-aware.

Next steps (short term):
- Stabilize the async prefetch pipeline and add metrics: per-page fetch latency, fetch success rate, prefetch cancellation rate.
- Add a lightweight calibration pass that runs 100 warmup tokens and derives layer_sensitivity heuristics automatically.
- Prototype a safe-mode fusion toggle that runs correctness comparisons on sample prompts in CI.
- Run larger scale experiments (4x A100) with mixed tenant workloads to measure fairness impact.

TODOs:
- [ ] Hook prefetch controller into global admission to make load-shedding decisions (Ethan)
- [ ] Add per-page telemetry and expose in console (Sofia)
- [ ] Add unit tests for fused index-remap kernel (Liam)

References & links:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2142 (proto implementation, async workers + events)
- JIRA: JIRA-RT-879 (paged-KV async experiments)
- Confluence notes: https://confluence.redwood/serving-runtime/kv-paging-experiments

Notes-to-self and rough ideas (scratchpad):
- Try heuristics where pages touched in last 2 turns get score boost; cheap but often effective for chat.
- Consider tiny dedicated NVMe buffer caches on host pinned memory for predicted hot pages to reduce host alloc churn.
- If we can get an L2 traversal hint from the model runtime (tokens predicted to be used), that would significantly improve prefetch hit-rate.

This doc will be iterated — main purpose is to capture prototype findings and next actionable items.
